title: Ruler Bench
context: Grade 4, the first working topic of the measures chapter. An adult sees things sorted and a ruler read, which a real ruler does perfectly well. What is actually being settled is which kind of measure a thing needs, why everyone must use the same unit, and where a measurement starts. The page tells the child to put one end at the zero mark. The ruler it prints carries no 0: its first mark is labelled with the unit, and its numbers begin at one. A child looking for a 0 starts at the one and gets a length one centimetre too long.

writeup.why: Sort each measure into its kind and its units, find out why handspans disagree, measure from the zero mark, and choose a unit before guessing a size.
writeup.look: A workbench: a tray of everyday things and three bins at the left, two hands at a bench top in the middle, and a ruler with no 0 at the right.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only: 'Ruler Bench' in ink at the far left, a small dot set clear of the name by measuring it, the phase title beside the dot on the same line, the host's navigation, and again, sound and restart as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at 64,108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: the things sorted, the readings taken or the cards filled against what this phase lays out, two numbers in ink, the first climbing by one as each thing settles in a bin, each reading is taken or each card is filled, and the second fixed at what this phase holds. On the second phase it holds only the handspans stamped with the hand showing, with no second number, because how many fit is the thing being found, and switching hands starts that hand's own count beside the first rather than clearing it. Nothing in it ever counts down and nothing in it ever reads as a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at 64,202. The thing tray lies along the top left of the working area, 520 by 90 at 64,214, holding a rope, a ribbon, a bag of flour, a bottle of water, a school bag and a spoon, each drawn plainly and apart. The three measure bins stand under it, each 164 by 170, at 64,318, 242,318 and 420,318, labelled length, weight and capacity in ink, with each bin's unit cards in a row along its foot: millimetres, centimetres, metres and kilometres; grams and kilograms; millilitres and litres. A thing dropped in a bin stays where it is dropped. A card lifted from one bin sticks only to a thing sorted into that bin; set on a thing in another bin it slides home to its own row, and that bin's label lights. The bench top runs along the foot of the left half, 520 by 56 at 64,540, with the hand switch under it, 250 by 56 at 64,612, showing a large hand and a small hand. Each tap stamps one handspan of the chosen hand along the bench as a sky blue outline, the large hand's stamps in a row above the bench and the small hand's in a row below it, so the two rows stand one over the other and neither is cleared. The centimetre tape lies coiled at the bench's right end. Pulled, it runs along the bench with its zero mark vermilion at the bench's left end, and its reading in centimetres is written at the bench's right end; it gives that one reading whichever hand's row is showing. At the right of the working area the ruler lies across, 540 by 70 at 600,300: fifteen centimetres, a long near-black tick at every centimetre and a short one at every half, the numerals one to fifteen above the long ticks, and the first tick carrying the letters cm and no numeral, as the chapter's own ruler does. That first tick is the zero mark, and it lights vermilion whenever an object's end sits on it. The object slider sits above the ruler, 540 by 76 at 600,214, holding one object at a time, a crayon, an eraser, a key or a pencil, which slides along the ruler half a centimetre at a time and settles with its left end on a tick; the tick under its right end is the reading mark and lights vermilion. With the left end on the zero mark, the reading is the length. With it on any other tick, a near-black bracket opens under the ruler and counts the centimetre spaces the object covers, one at a time from its left end, a half space counted as a half, and the count is written in sky blue beside the reading. The estimate card and the measure card sit under the ruler side by side, each 250 by 80, at 600,400 and 890,400, each with a unit tag, and once both are filled a reddish purple bar between them, drawn to scale, shows the gap. The unit picker stands under them, 540 by 150 at 600,520, offering three sizes for one thing, such as centimetres, metres or kilometres, each with a small picture beside it: a fingertip across a centimetre, one big step for a metre, and a road between two towns for a kilometre. Down the right of the canvas, in the same rectangle on every phase and never animated in or out, the question sits above the answer slot at 1186,250 (356 by 92) that holds what the child has given, and under it the pad at 1170,368 (388 by 363). The pad is twelve number keys three across, with a unit tag under the slot naming the unit the answer is in, filled in beside the number and never left off. It has no dot key. On the first phase a word pad sits over it with keys reading length, weight and capacity; on the second, keys reading the hands differ, the bench changed and a child miscounted; on the third the slot is a measure in centimetres with a millimetres box beside it, for a reading that ends on a half mark; and on the fourth the unit tag becomes a picker of millimetres, centimetres, metres and kilometres. The footer runs 758 to 900: the voice caption at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling, and the phase bar at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Content colours are the chapter's own and are the pictures' colours too. The larger unit of any pair, kilometres beside metres, metres beside centimetres, centimetres beside millimetres, kilograms and litres, is deep blue wherever it is drawn: its digits in a column, a bar standing for whole units, or a kilogram weight. The smaller unit of the pair, and the part left over after the whole units, is green: metres beside kilometres, centimetres beside metres, millimetres, grams and millilitres. One larger unit carried from the smaller column, or broken into smaller units to borrow, and every digit that move rewrites, is amber. A zero that fills an empty place of the smaller unit is grey. What is left after taking away, and the difference between two measures, is reddish purple. A count of things, handspans, glasses, jars, pourings or bags, is sky blue. The zero mark of a ruler or tape, and the mark where a reading is taken, are vermilion. Water and every other liquid is pale blue. Chrome never borrows one of those and none of them is ever used for chrome: every other tick and numeral on a ruler, and every rule, column line, bracket, strike line, table rule and panel edge, is near-black. Every reading survives with the colour taken away, because a unit is told apart by its column heading and its unit name, a padding zero by the box it sits in, a carried or broken unit by the chip it rides on, and a count by the slot that names what is counted, before any of them is told by a colour. Grey never means faint: a zero in the smaller unit's places is drawn at the same size and weight as every other digit and is never dimmed, shrunk or left out. A figure that goes down by one when a unit is broken is struck through once with the new figure written above it, and never rubbed out. No measure in two units is written as a decimal anywhere on the stage. The ruler shows no 0, as the chapter's does not, so the zero mark is found by where it is, the first tick, and not by a numeral. The bracket counts the spaces between ticks and not the ticks themselves, so the count it shows is the object's length in centimetres wherever the object lies.
writeup.finish: The card shows the three bins with the things the child sorted, the two handspan counts beside the tape reading, and the last object on the ruler with its estimate and measure.

phases.win: every thing settles in its bin wearing a unit of that kind, and a card of the wrong kind will not stick
phases.does: drops each thing in the bin for the measure asked, then gives it a unit card from that bin
phases.goal: length, weight and capacity each have their own units, and a thing's measure takes a unit of its own kind
phases.says: Is it a length, a weight or a capacity? Which units belong to it?
phases.check: Away from the screen: give one unit for how long a bus is, how heavy a bag of rice is, and how much a bucket holds.
phases.feels: each kind of measure has its own family of units, and a card from the wrong family will not stay on
phases.hands: Put a rope, a stone and a cup of water on a desk and ask how each could be measured. Sort the answers into three piles on the board, how long, how heavy and how much it holds, and write each pile's units under it: millimetres, centimetres, metres and kilometres; grams and kilograms; millilitres and litres. Then say a sentence with the wrong kind of unit, a rope six kilograms long, and let the class say what is wrong with it.
phases.tries: A miss is answered three ways at once and none of them is the answer. First rung, from the item's own miss line: is the question about how long, how heavy or how much it holds? Second rung, the phase's: which bin's cards can say that? Third rung: the tray is cut to one thing and one question, and the child sorts it before the other things come back. The word pad stays open behind all three rungs.

wrong.why: a bottle has a height, a weight and a capacity all at once, and its height is the one the eye meets first.
wrong.move: puts the bottle of water in the length bin, because the bottle is tall and its height is easy to see.
wrong.screen: the question's words, how much water it holds, light under the slot. The length bin's four cards are held up against those words one at a time, and none of them can say an amount of water; the capacity bin's two cards, millilitres and litres, then light beside it. The bottle stays in the bin where the child set it, nothing marked.

wrong.why: kilograms are a unit heard at many a shop counter, and a unit feels like a unit whatever it measures.
wrong.move: gives the rope a kilograms card, reaching for the unit heard most often at the shop.
wrong.screen: the card slides off the rope and home to the weight bin's row, and the length bin's label lights with its four cards. The tape then runs out along the rope, reading it in centimetres, a length's own unit, and the child's card stays lit in the weight bin's row, nothing marked.

phases.screen: the tray of things, the three bins, and the unit cards in a row
phases.soWhat: Length, weight and capacity each have their own units, and a measure takes a unit of its own kind.
phases.concept: A unit for every kind of measure

phases.win: the two handspan counts stand apart, and the tape gives one reading for both hands
phases.does: stamps handspans along the bench with each hand in turn, counts each, then runs the tape along it
phases.goal: handspans change from person to person, and a standard unit gives everyone the same reading
phases.says: Two hands, two counts. Now the tape. Does it matter whose hand lays it?
phases.check: Measure your desk in your own handspans, then ask a grown-up to do the same. Whose count is bigger, and why?
phases.feels: the bench stayed the same, and only the hand measuring it changed the count
phases.hands: Ask two children, one with a large hand and one with a small hand, to measure the same desk in handspans while the class counts aloud. Write both counts on the board and ask which is right. Let the class argue, then lay a measuring tape along the desk and read it once. Ask whether the tape's reading would change if the other child held it.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: did the bench change between the two counts? Second rung, the phase's: which hand fits more times along it? Third rung: the bench is cut short, and the child stamps both hands along it and reads the tape before the long bench comes back. The word pad stays open.

wrong.why: two different numbers for one bench sound as if one of them must be a mistake.
wrong.move: decides the child who counted nine handspans measured wrongly, because the other child counted only six for the same bench.
wrong.screen: both hands stamp along the one bench, the large hand's six outlines above it and the small hand's nine below it, and both rows end exactly at the bench's right end. The tape then runs along the bench and reads one hundred and eight centimetres, the same under either row, and the child's choice stays lit on the word pad, nothing marked.

wrong.why: a count of handspans sounds like a length, and nine is nine whoever says it.
wrong.move: tells a friend with a larger hand that a bench is nine handspans long, and expects the friend to make the same bench.
wrong.screen: the large hand stamps nine of its own handspans along a fresh strip laid beside the bench, and the strip runs past the bench's end by three of the large hand's spans. The tape reads the bench, one hundred and eight centimetres, and then the strip, one hundred and sixty-two, and both readings stay on the stage with the child's answer beside them.

phases.screen: one bench top with a large hand and a small hand beside it, and the centimetre tape coiled at one end
phases.soWhat: Handspans change from person to person, so standard units such as the centimetre are used. They give everyone the same reading.
phases.concept: Why everyone uses the same units

phases.win: the zero mark lights under the object's end, and the reading matches the count
phases.does: reads the other end, counts the centimetres the object covers, then slides it back to the first mark and reads again
phases.goal: a length is read from the zero mark, the first mark on the ruler, even where no 0 is printed
phases.says: Where does the ruler start? Count the centimetres it really covers.
phases.check: Away from the screen: a pencil lies with one end on the mark for two and the other on the mark for ten. How long is it?
phases.feels: the object did not grow when it sat on the mark for one; only the reading did
phases.hands: Hand out rulers and ask everyone to find the 0. Some rulers print one and some do not, like the chapter's. Show that the first mark is the zero mark whether or not a 0 is printed there. Then lay an eraser with one end on the mark for one, read the other end, and count the centimetre spaces it covers with a finger. Ask why the two numbers differ.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: where does the object's left end sit? Second rung, the phase's: which mark is the zero mark on this ruler? Third rung: the object is cut to one only a few centimetres long, and the child counts its spaces with the bracket before the longer object comes back. The number pad stays open.

wrong.why: no 0 is printed on this ruler, so the mark for one looks like the place a ruler starts.
wrong.move: reads nine for a crayon laid from the mark for one to the mark for nine, and gives nine centimetres as its length.
wrong.screen: the bracket opens under the crayon and counts the centimetre spaces it covers one at a time, eight of them, and writes eight in sky blue beside the reading of nine. The crayon then slides back until its left end sits on the first tick, which lights vermilion as the zero mark, and its other end now sits on eight. The child's nine stays in the slot beside it.

wrong.why: on this ruler numbers are printed only at the long marks, so the nearest printed number looks like the reading.
wrong.move: reads seven for a pencil laid from the zero mark whose far end lies on the short mark halfway between six and seven, giving the nearest printed number.
wrong.screen: the short mark under the pencil's end lights vermilion, halfway between the long marks for six and seven, and the bracket counts six whole centimetre spaces and then half of the seventh, drawn as half a space. The measure is written six centimetres five millimetres, because half of the ten millimetres in a centimetre is five, and the child's seven stays in the slot beside it.

phases.screen: the ruler with no numeral at its first mark, and an object lying with one end on the mark for one
phases.soWhat: Measure from the zero mark, the first mark on the ruler, even where no 0 is printed. Then the reading at the other end is the length.

phases.win: the estimate and the measure stand side by side, with the gap between them drawn as a short bar
phases.does: picks the unit that suits the thing, writes an estimate in it, then measures from the zero mark
phases.goal: a unit is chosen to suit the size before measuring or estimating
phases.says: Pick a unit that fits. Now guess. How close was your guess?
phases.check: Is a matchbox about five millimetres, five centimetres or five metres long? Guess first, then measure one.
phases.feels: the unit comes first, and a guess in that unit can then be held up against the measure
phases.hands: Hold up a matchbox, a door key and a school bag, and for each ask whether millimetres, centimetres, metres or kilometres would suit it. Then choose one thing, a pencil box, and let every child write an estimate with its unit before anyone measures. Measure it from the zero mark, and ask how close the guesses came, not who was right.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: how big is the thing, about a finger, a step or a journey? Second rung, the phase's: which unit's picture matches that size? Third rung: the picker is cut to two sizes, one plainly too small and one that fits, before the third comes back. The unit picker and the number pad stay open.

wrong.why: a classroom feels big to a child walking across it, and kilometres are the biggest unit on the list.
wrong.move: picks kilometres for the length of a classroom, because a classroom feels big to walk across.
wrong.screen: the picker lays its pictures beside the classroom: the road between two towns for a kilometre, with the classroom a small dot on it, and one big step for a metre. A metre stick is laid along the drawn classroom and fits eight times, and the child's kilometres stay lit on the picker, nothing marked.

wrong.why: a guess that differs from the measure feels like a wrong answer, and nobody wants a wrong answer on the card.
wrong.move: writes the estimate after measuring, or rubs it out and writes the measure in its place, so the gap comes to nothing.
wrong.screen: the estimate card locks once the measure card is filled, and a new number set on it is written on a fresh card beside the first, both kept. The gap bar is drawn from the first estimate, a pencil box guessed at twenty-five centimetres and measured at twenty-one, four centimetres, and the voice asks only how close it was.

phases.screen: one thing on the bench, the unit picker offering three sizes, and the estimate and measure cards empty
phases.soWhat: Choose a unit that suits the size, guess, then measure. A good estimate is a close one, and the gap tells how close.

writeup.delight: The third phase, the moment the object is slid from the mark for one back to the zero mark. The bracket under the ruler keeps its count, space for space, while both ends of the object glide one centimetre left together; the reading mark steps down one tick, the first tick lights vermilion, and the reading and the count come to the same number and hold. Slide it back to the mark for one and the reading climbs by one while the bracket's count does not move. It can be slid back and forth as often as a finger likes, nothing is marked, and the voice says nothing at all while it happens.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with nothing in front of it. On the first phase the tray holds its things and the three bins stand empty, each with its own unit cards in a row along its foot. On the second the bench top lies bare, with the large hand and the small hand beside it and the tape coiled at its right end. On the third an object already lies along the ruler with its left end on the mark for one, the reading mark at its other end unlit and the bracket folded away. On the fourth one thing stands on the bench beside the unit picker, and the estimate card and the measure card are both empty. The running count at the top left holds the things sorted, readings taken or cards filled against what this phase lays out, and the answer slot and the pad stand empty down the right. One thing moves, once: the first thing in the tray, or the small hand, or the ruler's first tick, the one with no numeral, or the unit picker, gives one slow pulse while the voice asks what kind of measure each thing needs. That pulse is the only invitation, and a finger on it is the whole way in.
writeup.freePlay: Any thing from the tray in any bin, the handspan bench with either hand, the ruler with any object, and the estimate cards open. Nothing to get right, no target and no timer. The child is left with the same stage and every control unlocked.
writeup.practice: Eight items over the four phases, easy first, on sorting measures and their units, handspans against centimetres, reading a ruler from its zero mark, and choosing a sensible unit for an estimate.
voiceLines: A bench of things to measure. What kind of measure does each one need?
Is it a length, a weight or a capacity? Which units belong to it?
Two hands, two counts. Now the tape. Does it matter whose hand lays it?
Where does the ruler start? Count the centimetres it really covers.
Pick a unit that fits. Now guess. How close was your guess?
A new thing. Decide what kind of measure it needs before you choose a unit.
Free play. Any thing, either hand, the ruler and the estimate cards, all open.
Look at what is being measured, then at where the measuring starts.
Every thing given a unit of its own kind, every reading taken from the zero mark, and every guess set beside a measure.

observations.why: A rope is measured for how long it is, and kilograms say how heavy something is.
observations.soWhat: Length, weight and capacity each have their own units, and a measure takes a unit of its own kind.
observations.observe: The kilograms card slid off the rope and went home to the weight bin.

observations.why: The bench did not change. A smaller handspan simply fits more times along it.
observations.soWhat: Handspans change from person to person, so standard units such as the centimetre are used.
observations.observe: The small hand's row held more stamps than the large hand's, and the tape gave one reading under both.

observations.why: The object's length never changed. Starting at the mark for one had moved both of its ends one centimetre along.
observations.soWhat: Measure from the zero mark, the first mark on the ruler, even where no 0 is printed.
observations.observe: Sliding the object back to the zero mark made the reading drop by one, while the bracket's count stayed the same.

observations.why: A guess and a measure in the same unit can be set side by side, and the gap is a length too.
observations.soWhat: Choose a unit that suits the size first, then guess, then measure, and see how close the guess was.
observations.observe: Once a unit was picked to suit the thing, the estimate and the measure stood in the same unit, with the gap drawn between them.

source_tool.description: A workbench fills the stage. At the left a tray holds everyday things, a rope, a ribbon, a bag of flour, a bottle of water and a spoon, and three bins stand behind it labelled length, weight and capacity, each with its own unit cards: millimetres, centimetres, metres and kilometres; grams and kilograms; millilitres and litres. A thing sorted into a bin can take only that bin's units. In the middle one bench top is measured twice, once by a large hand and once by a small one, and each handspan is stamped along it and counted; a centimetre tape then runs along the same bench and gives one reading, whichever hand lays it. At the right a fifteen centimetre ruler is drawn as the page draws it, its first mark carrying no numeral and its numbers running from one. An object slides along it. When its end sits on the first mark, the zero mark lights and the reading at the other end is the length; when its end sits on the mark for one, a bracket counts the centimetres the object really covers, and the reading is seen to be one too many. An estimate card and a measure card sit under the ruler side by side, and the gap between them is drawn as a bar. A unit picker offers three sizes for one thing, such as centimetres, metres or kilometres, with a small picture of each size beside it.
source_tool.art_direction: Bins, two hands and a plain ruler / Picture book

stage.note: Every coordinate is authored in 1600x900, so a smartboard and a phone in landscape get one composition. Nothing scrolls. The three bands below are the settled layout, taken from Two Hundred Trail in Class 3 chapter 3 once it was finished; a tool that has to depart from one of them says in its own writeup.stage which band it changed and why.

bands.canvas: 92 to 746. One rounded panel holding everything the child works on.
bands.footer: 758 to 900. The voice at the far left, the phase bar at the right.
bands.header: 0 to 80. One line, and only one.

zones.bar: the phase bar at the right of the footer, the question count under it
zones.pad: under the slot, and furniture on every phase: twelve keys three across where a number is asked for, a word pad where a name or a rule is
zones.name: the tool name at the far left of the header, a measured dot set clear of it
zones.runs: the running count, on the canvas at its top left, never up in the chrome. It counts the thing the tool is actually building; where a tool has nothing to count that corner carries the record being kept instead, and that tool's own stage says so
zones.slot: the question and the child's answer, fixed down the right of the canvas
zones.work: the working area, one thousand and eighty-six by five hundred and twenty-eight
zones.title: the phase title beside that dot, on the same single header line
zones.voice: the caption at the far left of the footer, its speaking dot beside it

stage.furniture: The working area is furnished from the first frame. What waits for the child is the count, not the picture: the panels, the slot and the pad are all up and empty before anything is asked.
stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare, because the working area is the tool.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box anywhere on the stage. The score leaves on the finished event and it is the host that decides whether to show it, so a child working is never watching a number that judges them.

style.motion: Animate only what carries meaning. Anything that is not changing does not move. Every reward is the maths itself moving, never confetti. Honour prefers-reduced-motion.
drawing: Hand-built inline SVG. No assets and no network, so a school cart works offline.
Chunky rounded forms and large touch targets. A finger is the pointer, not a mouse.

Drawn things, not abstract boxes: a workbench with a tray of everyday things, a fifteen centimetre ruler, a ladder of units, a column frame with a unit switch, a pan balance with iron weights, a tap, jugs, glasses, jars, bottles and a tank.

A ruler is drawn as the page draws it: a long tick at every centimetre and a short one at every half, the numerals one to fifteen, and a first tick carrying the unit name and no numeral. That first tick is the zero mark and lights as one.
Every measure is written with its unit named, the larger unit on the left and the smaller on the right, as in 4 km 66 m. A measure in two units is never written as a decimal on any stage.

The smaller unit's places are fixed boxes: three beside kilometres, kilograms and litres, two beside metres and one beside centimetres. A zero filling one of those boxes is drawn at full size and weight and is never dimmed or dropped.

A number that joins two units is shown beside them wherever the child works with them: ten between millimetres and centimetres, a hundred between centimetres and metres, and a thousand between metres and kilometres, grams and kilograms, and millilitres and litres. Weight and capacity carry one number only, a thousand.
What is left after dividing is drawn in its own slot in the smaller unit, at full strength, and it is never folded into the quotient.

A larger unit broken to borrow is drawn as exactly the joining number of smaller pieces: ten pieces for a centimetre, a hundred for a metre, and a thousand for a kilometre, a kilogram or a litre, the thousand drawn as ten bars of a hundred.
No count, reading or result is shown before the child makes it. A jar count appears only once the pouring is done, and a reading only once the object is laid.
Every word on the stage says weight, the vocabulary box's word, for how heavy a thing is.
A container whose capacity is shown is drawn full to its brim.
Two measures being compared stand on the stage at the same time, one beside or above the other. An answer that has been replaced is never cleared away.
style.palette_rule: A chrome colour never fills a digit, a bar, a weight or a liquid the child is reading, and a content colour is never used for chrome. These are the chapter's own colours, taken from the pictures, so a tool and a picture of the same thing are the same colour. The larger unit of any pair, kilometres beside metres, metres beside centimetres, centimetres beside millimetres, kilograms and litres, is deep blue wherever it is drawn: its digits in a column, a bar standing for whole units, or a kilogram weight. The smaller unit of the pair, and the part left over after the whole units, is green. One larger unit carried from the smaller column, or broken into smaller units to borrow, and every digit that move rewrites, is amber. A zero that pads the smaller unit's places, as in zero seven five, is grey, drawn at the same size and weight as every other digit and never faded, because it is holding a place. What is left after taking away, and the difference between two measures, is reddish purple. A count of things, handspans, glasses, jars, pourings or bags, is sky blue. The zero mark of a ruler or tape and the mark where a reading is taken are vermilion. Water and every other liquid is pale blue. Every other tick and numeral on a ruler, and every rule, column line, bracket and table rule, is near-black chrome. All of that holds in greyscale, because each unit is told apart by its column heading and its unit name, a padding zero by the box it sits in, and a carried or broken unit by the chip it rides on, before any of them is told apart by colour.

rules: Every spoken line is also printed in the caption line at the far left of the footer, so a muted tablet and a child who cannot hear lose nothing.
The caption stays in the footer. Nothing is ever written over the working area.

Numbers are written as words in every line and never as digits, so the voice says four steps and not 4 steps. Handed a digit, a synthesiser reads it in whatever register it likes and the chapter loses the words it is teaching.
The voice never gives the answer. It asks the same question a different way.
It speaks on opening, once when a phase begins, on a miss, and at the finish. It is silent otherwise; a tool that chatters gets muted, and then the first rule is all that is left.
props.muted is honoured at the source, and turning sound off cancels any line already speaking.
voice.where: The caption line sits at the far left of the footer with a small dot beside it that glows while the voice is talking. An again control repeats the last line.
voice.figure: None. The voice speaks with nothing on the stage.
voice.onMiss: Look at what is being measured, then at where the measuring starts.
voice.onNext: A new thing. Decide what kind of measure it needs before you choose a unit.
voice.opening: A bench of things to measure. What kind of measure does each one need?
voice.onFinish: Every thing given a unit of its own kind, every reading taken from the zero mark, and every guess set beside a measure.
voice.onFreePlay: Free play. Any thing, either hand, the ruler and the estimate cards, all open.
voice.figure_rule: A figure appears only where the printed chapter puts one and it has work to do. Everywhere else the voice speaks from the caption line with nothing on the stage: a mascot with no job is one more thing competing with the quantities the child is looking at.
voice.voicePreference: an English voice, female where one is offered

phase_map.concept: A unit for every kind of measure
Why everyone uses the same units

placement.where: After the class has measured one desk in handspans and compared the counts, and has looked for the 0 on a real ruler. The tool slides an object's end onto the mark for one and shows the reading come out a centimetre too long. A ruler on a desk lets that pass unnoticed.

answer_key.rule: Length is measured in millimetres, centimetres, metres and kilometres, weight in grams and kilograms, and capacity in millilitres and litres. A thing's measure takes a unit of its own kind: the length of a rope is never given in kilograms. Handspans, footsteps, cubits and paces change from person to person, so standard units are used, and they give everyone the same reading. A length is measured by laying one end of the object on the zero mark of the ruler and reading the mark at the other end. The zero mark is the first mark on the ruler, even where no 0 is printed there. A unit is chosen to suit the size before measuring or estimating: millimetres or centimetres for small things, metres for a room, kilometres between towns.
answer_key.wrong: The object slides back to the first mark, the zero mark lights, and the centimetres are counted one at a time from there to the other end. Nothing is cleared and nothing is marked.

hostProps.muted: Sound off. Honour it at the source, not by muting an element later. The captions carry on.
hostProps.phase: number, 1-based, which phase to build. The host chooses the activity; the component builds that phase and nothing else and never moves on by itself.
hostProps.device: tablet / web / smartboard. The stage is a fixed 1600x900 that scales; lay nothing out per device.
hostProps.audience: classroom or solo, and ACCEPTED AND NOT ACTED ON. The teach run and the hint ladder run either way. Kept so the contract is one shape across the book, and named here so nobody reads the shape as a promise.
hostProps.learnQuestions: The four worked items, one per phase, supplied by the host.
hostProps.practiceQuestions: The eight practice items, supplied by the host.

phase_mount.run: A phase is a complete activity in itself and it runs once. The teaching and the doing are not two screens and not two modes: the stage is furnished once, the voice talks over it, and the child starts working on the same stage without anything being rebuilt. Whatever the tool as a whole has to say goes into the FIRST phase's teach run, because there is no opening screen to say it on.
phase_mount.idle: NO AUTO-ADVANCE. After firing, the tool goes idle on the settled phase with the child's work still on it, and stops. Where the host supplies onNext it is drawn and it calls the host back; nothing in the component advances a phase.
phase_mount.prop: phase: number, 1-based, matching writeup.phases[].n. Rounded, clamped, and defaulting to 1 when the host sends nothing, so a bare mount is still a working tool rather than a blank screen. Read once: changing which phase a mount shows is a re-mount.
phase_mount.rule: ONE PHASE, ONE MOUNT. The host says which phase to build by passing `phase`, and the component builds that phase and nothing else. It does not know what came before it and it never moves on by itself.
phase_mount.opening: There is no opening panel and no Start button. The host has already chosen the activity, and a cover screen in front of it is a click between a child and the work. writeup.opening is the first frame of every mount rather than a panel of its own.
phase_mount.completion: The terminal event `finished`, with the phase in its detail, fired exactly once and guarded by a one-shot ref that only a restart re-arms, with the chime and the settle OUTSIDE the guard. props.onComplete is called alongside it: the event is the platform's signal and the callback is the host wrapper's, and firing only one of them leaves a child on a tool that never completes.
phase_mount.notInAMount: No finish card and no free play. Both are the host's now, built out of what the events told it. writeup.finish and writeup.freePlay stay as the record of what they are.

shared_state.note: What getState() returns. These names are a contract: the host reads them to persist and resume a child mid-activity, so renaming one breaks resume. `mode` is gone from this list because there is no mode. `phase` is the phase the host mounted, so a resume restores the work inside a phase and the host restores which phase.

agent_control.reason: Every tool in this chapter is child-operated. There is no agent-driven Concept mode, no postMessage command channel and no narration the tool waits on; the adult, where there is one, talks over the tool rather than through it.

steps: A rope is measured for how long it is, which is a length: millimetres, centimetres, metres or kilometres.
A bag is measured for how heavy it is, which is a weight: grams or kilograms.
The milk is measured for how much liquid there is, which is a capacity: millilitres or litres.
items.answer: The rope needs a length, in metres; the bag needs a weight, in kilograms; the milk needs a capacity, in litres or millilitres
items.question: A skipping rope, a school bag and a jug of milk are to be measured. Which kind of measure does each need, and which unit could each take?
items.checkpoint: Each kind of measure has its own units: length in mm, cm, m and km, weight in g and kg, capacity in mL and L.
items.misconception: Giving a measure a unit of the wrong kind, such as writing the bag's weight in centimetres or the milk in metres.

steps: The bench is the same length for both children.
A smaller hand fits more times along it, so the child with the smaller hand counts 12.
A handspan changes from person to person, so a standard unit such as the centimetre is used, and it gives everyone one reading.
items.answer: Both counted correctly with their own hands. Their hands are different sizes, so the counts differ, and a centimetre tape gives both of them the same length
items.question: Two children measure the same bench with their hands. One counts 9 handspans and the other counts 12. Which count is right?
items.checkpoint: Handspans, footsteps and cubits change from person to person; standard units give everyone the same answer.
items.misconception: Deciding that one child counted wrongly, or that the bench changed, when only the size of the hand changed.

steps: The first mark on the ruler is the zero mark, even though no 0 is printed there.
The crayon's left end sits on the zero mark, so the reading at its right end is its length.
The right end is on the mark for 7, so the crayon is 7 cm long.
items.question: A crayon lies along a ruler. Its left end is on the first mark, which has no 0 printed on it, and its right end is on the mark for 7. How long is the crayon?
items.checkpoint: Measure from the zero mark, the first mark on the ruler, and read the mark at the other end.
items.misconception: Looking for a 0, not finding one, and laying the end on the mark for 1, which makes a length read one centimetre too long.

steps: 10 cm is about the width of a hand, far too small for a bus.
10 km is a long journey, far too big for a bus.
A metre is about one big step, so 10 m is about ten big steps, which suits a bus.
items.question: Is a school bus about 10 cm, 10 m or 10 km long?
items.checkpoint: Choose a unit that suits the size: centimetres for small things, metres for a room or a bus, kilometres between towns.
items.misconception: Picking centimetres because the number 10 is small, instead of asking how big the thing is.

learn.shape: Worked items, shown solved, mandatory before practice unlocks.
learn.selection: Fixed order, walking the phases from the first to the last.
learn.content_criterion: One per phase, so Learn walks the whole topic and stops.

items.question: Which unit fits the gap: a bucket holds 12 ___ of water? Choose from cm, kg and L.
items.final_answer: L, because how much water a bucket holds is a capacity

items.question: Say which kind of measure each is, and give each a unit: the weight of a bag of rice, the length of a ribbon, the juice in a glass.
items.final_answer: The rice is a weight, in kg; the ribbon is a length, in cm or m; the juice is a capacity, in mL

items.question: A grown-up measures a table as 6 handspans and a child measures it as 9 handspans. Why are the numbers different?
items.final_answer: Their hands are different sizes, so the same table takes more of the child's handspans. A standard unit such as the centimetre gives one answer

items.question: Why is cloth sold by the metre and not by the handspan?
items.final_answer: A metre is the same for everyone, so the seller and the buyer get the same length. Handspans change from person to person

items.question: A pencil's left end is on the first mark of a ruler, where no 0 is printed. Its right end is at 12. How long is the pencil?
items.final_answer: 12 cm, because the first mark is the zero mark

items.question: A child lays a key with one end on the mark for 1 and reads 6 at the other end. How long is the key?
items.final_answer: 5 cm. From the mark for 1 to the mark for 6 is five centimetres; laid from the zero mark, its other end would sit at 5

items.question: Is a cricket pitch about 20 cm, 20 m or 20 km long?
items.final_answer: About 20 m. 20 cm is about the length of a new pencil, and 20 km is a long journey

items.question: A child estimates a notebook to be 30 cm long, then measures it from the zero mark and finds 24 cm. By how much was the estimate out?
items.final_answer: By 6 cm; the estimate was 6 cm too long

practice.selection: Fixed order, easy first, and every phase represented.
practice.interaction_rules: Answered on the tool itself. A wrong answer returns the question with a hint; nothing is marked and retries are unlimited.

student_controls.effect: holds the everyday things to be sorted and measured
length, weight and capacity, each taking only its own unit cards
mm, cm, m, km, g, kg, mL and L, each sticking only to a thing in its own bin
measures the bench top in large handspans or small ones
runs along the bench top and gives one reading for every hand
a fifteen centimetre ruler whose first mark carries no numeral
moves an object along the ruler and sets the mark its end sits on
hold a guess and a reading side by side, with the gap drawn between them

teaching_notes: Measure one desk in handspans before the tool is opened, with a large hand and a small one, and let the class argue over the two counts before a tape settles them. That is why standard units are used. Then hand out real rulers and ask where the 0 is. The page says to lay one end at the zero mark, and the ruler it draws prints no 0: its first mark carries the unit's name and its numbers start at one. Say that the first mark is the zero mark wherever a ruler leaves the 0 off. Then have a child lay an eraser from the mark for one and see the reading come out a centimetre too long. The recap on the opening page asks for a unit in each of fifteen sentences. Its list leaves out millimetres, and three of its sizes are poor guides: a door four metres high, a pencil four centimetres long and a carton of cricket balls weighing thirty kilograms. The units are still the right ones; ask the class whether the sizes are. The chapter's first sentence says each higher unit is ten times bigger, which holds only for millimetres and centimetres, so do not repeat it here. The next topic gives each step its own number. The estimate table asks for a guess and then a measure. Write both, and ask how close the guess was rather than whether it was right.
generation_prompt: Build a measuring bench on a fixed 1600x900 SVG stage. At the left of the working area a tray holds everyday things, a rope, a ribbon, a bag of flour, a bottle of water, a school bag and a spoon, with three bins behind it labelled length, weight and capacity. Each bin carries its own unit cards, mm, cm, m and km for length, g and kg for weight, and mL and L for capacity, and a card from one bin will not attach to a thing sorted into another. In the middle one bench top is drawn with a large hand and a small hand beside it; each tap stamps one handspan of the chosen hand along the bench and counts it, and a centimetre tape runs along the same bench and gives one reading, whichever hand lays it. At the right a fifteen centimetre ruler is drawn with a long tick at every centimetre and a short tick at every half, its first tick carrying the letters cm and no numeral, and the numerals one to fifteen above the other long ticks. An object can be slid along the ruler. When its end sits on the first tick, that tick lights as the zero mark and the reading at the other end is shown as the length; when its end sits on any other tick, a bracket counts the centimetres the object really covers and shows the count beside the reading. Under the ruler an estimate card and a measure card sit side by side, with a short bar drawn for the gap between them. A unit picker offers three sizes for one thing, with a small picture beside each. Pointer events only, no assets, no network. Build it from the writeup and the tool build spec, not from this paragraph (maths_agent/TOOL_BUILD_SPEC.md). The three bands and every measurement come from writeup.stage and tool_config.style.stage: one header line, one canvas panel holding everything the child works on with the running count at its top left and the question, slot and pad fixed down its right as furniture, and a footer with the voice at the far left and the phase bar at the right. No sidebar, and no score box anywhere. One phase, one mount: build the phase the host passes and nothing else (tool_config.phase_mount). The first frame comes from writeup.opening. Each phase comes from writeup.phases, with its screen, action, reward and spoken line; its tries field is the hint ladder and its wrong list is what the stage does about a wrong answer, redrawn in steps on the working area with nothing marked and nothing reset. The one surprise is writeup.delight. The look and the sounds come from tool_config.style, voice and audio.
instructions_for_student: Put each thing in the bin for its kind. Give it a unit from that bin. Lay the object's end on the first mark. That mark is the zero mark. Read the other end. Pick a unit, then guess, then measure.
